Appendix C Significance Summary

All significance tests use paired bootstrap resampling (B=10,000B=10{,}000). For SocialClaimSplit-100, base →\to all improvements are significant for Qwen3-8B (Semantic-F1 and AVR, both p<10−4p<10^{-4}) and Phi-3-mini (Semantic-F1 p=0.002p=0.002, AVR p=0.003p=0.003). For WikiSplitBench-1000, Qwen3-8B improves AVR significantly (p<10−4p<10^{-4}) while Semantic-F1 remains statistically unchanged (p=0.492p=0.492). Gemini Flash shows no significant base →\to all shift on WikiSplitBench-1000 (Semantic-F1 p=0.411p=0.411, AVR p=0.821p=0.821). For ClaimDecompBench-1000, Qwen3-8B improves both Semantic-F1 and AVR significantly (both p<10−4p<10^{-4}).

Appendix D Rule Repair Convergence Analysis

Under Assumption 1, Theorem T1 shows that nviol{}_{\text{viol}} (compound-boundary count) is non-increasing under rule repair; AVR may fluctuate locally when splitting a multi-conjunction claim creates two still-violating children, but converges empirically in a single pass. We empirically verify that a single pass is sufficient in practice. Starting from the base decomposition (no repair), we apply the rule repairer k∈{1,2,3}k\in\{1,2,3\} times on WikiSplitBench-100 for all four models and record AVR, RR, and Semantic-F1.

The rule repairer applies pattern-matching splits (conservative_split, _split_reporting_because, _split_used_to_and) followed by deduplication. These transforms are idempotent by construction: once a claim has been split or deduplicated, re-application cannot further reduce it. Consequently, no example among the 4×100=4004\times 100=400 tested cases shows any AVR or RR reduction in pass 2 relative to pass 1. The single-pass design of CREDENCE is thus empirically optimal for rule repair. Semantic-F1 also remains within ±0.4\pm 0.4 pp of the base value across all models, confirming that conservative splitting does not compromise semantic coverage.

Extending this analysis to the full 8,800-example evaluation across four benchmark variants and four models, Table 14 reports the two largest cross-domain variants, with the remaining variants provided in the artifact JSON. Pass-2 and pass-3 provide zero improvement in all cases (0/8,800 examples), confirming that the single-pass design is sufficient across domains and scales. Six examples (0.07%0.07\%) exhibit a nominal AVR increase after pass 1, attributed to dep-parser edge cases consistent with the 1%1\% sm/trf disagreement rate reported below.

Parser reliability.

The above analysis relies on en_core_web_sm as a practical surrogate for the oracle parser assumed in Theorem 1. In practice, en_core_web_sm never raises a parse exception on our data (0/1,000 sampled claims), and agrees with the more accurate en_core_web_trf transformer model on 99.0% of 200 sampled claims (2 disagreements: one false positive on a how-clause, one false negative on a copular construction). Theorem 4.1 monotonicity holds on all 1,000 sampled examples (100.00%), and on 8,794/8,800 full-dataset examples (99.93%), with 6 edge-case violations (0.07%0.07\%) attributable to these parser disagreements.

Appendix E Encoder Sensitivity of Semantic-F1

Semantic-F1 uses BGE-large (bge-large-en-v1.5) as the default sentence encoder. To assess whether results depend on this choice, we re-compute Semantic-F1 with two alternative encoders—all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (MiniLM; 22M parameters) and intfloat/e5-base-v2 (E5-base; 109M parameters)— on all 35,200 examples from the 64 evaluation JSONL files (4 benchmark variants × 4 models × 4 pipeline modes, 100–1000 examples each: Social-100, WikiSplitBench-100, WikiSplitBench-1000, ClaimDecompBench-1000). All computation ran on CPU with sentence caching (44,333 unique sentences encoded once and reused).

We compare per-example Semantic-F1 scores against the pre-stored BGE-large values using Pearson rr, Spearman ρ\rho, and model ranking preservation.

Model ranking preservation.

For each (dataset, pipeline mode) combination, we compute the mean Semantic-F1 per model and check whether the pairwise ranking of models is preserved relative to BGE-large. There are 72 such pairs across all conditions. MiniLM preserves 71/72 pairs (98.6%); E5-base preserves 70/72 (97.2%). The single discordant pair in each case involves two models with virtually identical mean Semantic-F1 values (<<0.3 pp apart), where rank order is practically irrelevant.

Table 15 shows that both lighter encoders correlate strongly with BGE-large (r≥0.92r\geq 0.92, ρ≥0.92\rho\geq 0.92). MiniLM produces Semantic-F1 values that are on average 3.8 pp lower than BGE-large (reflecting its smaller capacity), while E5-base produces values 5.3 pp higher (reflecting its different training objective with explicit query–passage prefix supervision). The important finding is that these offsets are systematic: they compress or expand the absolute scale without changing relative model comparisons. Consequently, all inter-model and inter-mode rankings reported in the main paper (Tables 3, 4, and 6) are robust to encoder choice; only the absolute Semantic-F1 numbers would shift by a constant offset if a different encoder were substituted.

Per-dataset, correlation is highest on SocialClaimSplit-100 (r≥0.97r\geq 0.97) where conjunction-split claims have high lexical overlap making embedding choice less critical, and slightly lower on ClaimDecompBench-1000 (r≈0.87r\approx 0.87–0.890.89) where greater paraphrase diversity means the two encoders weight token synonymy differently.

Similarity function robustness.

We additionally verify robustness to the similarity function choice. Replacing cosine with Tanimoto similarity (T⁡(a,b)=a⋅b/(‖a‖2+‖b‖2−a⋅b)T(a,b)=a\cdot b\,/\,(\|a\|^{2}+\|b\|^{2}-a\cdot b), a magnitude-aware alternative) yields Pearson r=0.996r=0.996 and Spearman ρ=0.998\rho=0.998 against the cosine baseline across 400 examples (Table 16). For unit-norm BGE embeddings, Tanimoto is a strictly monotone transformation of cosine (T=cos⁡θ/(2−cos⁡θ)T=\cos\theta\,/\,(2-\cos\theta)), so all within-group rankings are analytically preserved. Absolute scores shift by ≈7.8\approx 7.8 pp on average but do not alter any comparative conclusion.

Repair-metric coupling test.

To verify that Semantic-F1 improvements are not inflated by using the same BGE-large encoder for both repair decisions and evaluation, we re-ran the repair stage (repair mode) on SocialClaimSplit-100 with an E5-base encoder (intfloat/e5-base) for internal repair decisions, while keeping BGE-large for evaluation. The resulting Δ\Delta Semantic-F1 between the two conditions was +0.0000+0.0000 (Table 17), below the 0.02 threshold for meaningful coupling confound. We conclude that metric–system coupling does not materially inflate the reported results.

The large verify_ok drop (0.9000→0.45000.9000\to 0.4500) reflects verifier-threshold sensitivity to different internal repair trajectories under encoder swap, not a change in final decomposition quality under external evaluation. Importantly, the endpoint quality metrics used for conclusions remain stable (Δ\Delta Semantic-F1 =+0.0000=+0.0000; Δ\Delta AVR =+0.0000=+0.0000), so we treat this as a calibration-shift effect in pass/fail gating rather than evidence of inflated Semantic-F1 gains.

Verdict: NOT_CONFOUNDED (threshold |Δ|\Delta Semantic-F1|≤0.02|\leq 0.02).

Appendix F Gating False Negative Analysis

The pipeline’s gating logic preserves the base decomposition whenever the verifier reports no violations (verify_ok = True), avoiding unnecessary repair. A “gating false negative” (FN) occurs when the verifier accepts the base output but the underlying AVR is non-trivial (AVR>0.01\text{AVR}>0.01) — the gating “trusts” a decomposition that is technically imperfect.

We quantify FN rates across 8,800 examples (4 models ×\times 4 benchmark variants in base vs. repair mode) by comparing base and repair predictions: an example is classified as gated when base and repair predictions are identical, and as a FN when gated despite AVR>0.01\text{AVR}>0.01.

Gated% vs. base verify_ok%. Gated% is not equivalent to base verify_ok%. Gated% measures output identity between base and repair branches after pipeline execution, while verify_ok% measures whether base passes verifier constraints before repair. A model can have high verify_ok% but low Gated% if repair still triggers output changes on many borderline cases due to thresholding and post-check logic.

Results.

Table 18 summarises gating rates and FN rates across all four models. The overall FN rate is 9.5% (836/8,800 examples). Gemini Flash exhibits the lowest FN rate (1.5%), consistent with its higher base decomposition quality, while open-weight models range from 10–15%.

The mean AVR of FN examples is 0.42, confirming that these are genuine (non-trivial) violations rather than threshold artefacts. The 9.5% FN rate represents the upper bound on examples where an additional repair pass could be beneficial; in practice, the single-pass design (Section 3.3) was chosen to favour precision over recall in repair, avoiding the hallucination risk associated with unnecessary LLM interventions on already acceptable decompositions.

Appendix G Tau-dup Threshold Sensitivity

The Redundancy Rate (RR) metric uses a cosine similarity threshold τdup\tau_{\mathrm{dup}} to flag near-duplicate claims: two predicted claims are considered redundant if their BGE-large cosine similarity exceeds τdup\tau_{\mathrm{dup}}.

The deployed value is τdup=0.92\tau_{\mathrm{dup}}=0.92 based on validation ablations reported below (Figure 6). while avoiding over-aggressive merging of topically-similar but informationally-distinct claims.

To assess sensitivity, we post-hoc recompute RR on all 8,400 base predictions across three datasets (τ∈{0.80,0.85,0.90,0.95}\tau\in\{0.80,0.85,0.90,0.95\}), which brackets the deployed value of 0.920.92, fixing all other metrics to their pre-stored values.

Lowering τ\tau to 0.80 inflates RR by ++10–11 pp, flagging many semantically distinct claims that share topical vocabulary as false-positive duplicates. For example, at τ=0.80\tau=0.80, two claims about the same entity from different angles (“X was born in 1921” and “X reigned from 1927”) can exceed the threshold, despite conveying distinct information. Raising τ\tau to 0.95 deflates RR by 2–3 pp, causing genuine near-paraphrase duplicates to be missed (e.g., “X said Y” and “According to X, Y”). Semantic-F1 is unaffected by threshold choice (±0.000\pm 0.000 pp) since it is computed from pre-stored embeddings independently. The deployed τ=0.92\tau=0.92 lies in the flat regime between 0.900.90 and 0.950.95, representing the optimal operating point: it avoids the false-positive inflation of τ≤0.85\tau\leq 0.85 while remaining sensitive to genuine near-paraphrase patterns such as “X said Y” vs. “According to X, Y” (cosine similarity ≈0.93\approx 0.93–0.950.95 in BGE-large space). This value is selected from the ablation above as the empirical operating point that avoids false-positive inflation while remaining sensitive to genuine near-paraphrase patterns; it is confirmed as the deployed default in acd/metrics.py (MetricSuite(dup_thr=0.92)).

Appendix H Metric–Human Preference Alignment Study

Setup.

To assess whether Semantic-F1 better tracks human decomposition preference than Jaccard-F1, we ran a pairwise preference study over discriminative pairs where the two metrics disagree. Each pair compares two genuine decompositions of the same input from different models (model X vs model Y), with both options constrained to npred≥2n_{\mathrm{pred}}\geq 2. Five annotator files were collected; after resolving schema/ID mismatch, 82 mapped pairs were available for metric-alignment analysis.

Results.

Table 19 reports Kendall τ\tau between each metric’s ranking and human preference (majority vote).

Additional reportable signals:

  • •

    Semantic-F1 matches majority preference on 45 pairs vs 34 for Jaccard-F1 (3 majority ties; exclusive-win sign test p=0.2604).

  • •

    Inter-annotator agreement on shared IAA items: Fleiss’ κ=0.619\kappa=0.619.

  • •

    Annotation confidence is high/medium for 119/121 labelled decisions.

Preference Study shows a consistent directional advantage of Semantic-F1 over Jaccard-F1 in human-alignment metrics (Δ​τ=+0.2679\Delta\tau=+0.2679), with moderate inter-annotator reliability (Fleiss’ κ=0.619\kappa=0.619). While the current sample size is underpowered for strong significance claims, the trend indicates Semantic-F1 as a potentially more discriminative proxy rather than a statistically conclusive superiority claim.
